scenarios.title: Smoke Under the Door
scenarios.description: You're in your office and you smell smoke. There's no alarm yet, but smoke is drifting in from under the door to the hallway.

choices.text: Open the door quickly and look into the hallway
choices.feedback: Never open a door without checking it first. If fire is on the other side, a sudden rush of air can cause a dangerous flashover. Always check before opening.

choices.text: Feel the door and handle with the back of your hand before opening
choices.feedback: Correct. Checking a door's heat before opening tells you if fire is close on the other side. If it's hot, keep it shut and find another way out.

choices.text: Ignore it and keep working, assuming it's nothing
choices.feedback: Smoke should never be ignored. It spreads fast and is more dangerous than the flames themselves. Treat any smoke as a sign to act immediately.

scenarios.title: The Alarm Sounds
scenarios.description: The fire alarm goes off. You're on the 6th floor and need to get outside. The elevator is right next to you.

choices.text: Take the elevator down since it's faster
choices.feedback: Elevators can stop working or trap you between floors during a fire, and shafts can fill with smoke. Always use the stairs during a fire evacuation.

choices.text: Use the stairwell and head to the nearest exit
choices.feedback: Correct. Stairwells are built to stay safer during fires. Knowing at least two exit routes in advance makes this decision automatic under pressure.

choices.text: Stay at your desk and wait for someone to give instructions
choices.feedback: Waiting wastes critical time. Once an alarm sounds, treat it as real and begin evacuating right away rather than waiting for confirmation.

scenarios.title: Smoke-Filled Corridor
scenarios.description: You open a safe exit door and find the corridor filling with thick smoke. You need to reach the stairwell at the end of the hall.

choices.text: Stay low and crawl toward the stairwell
choices.feedback: Correct. Smoke rises, so the air near the floor stays clearer and cooler for longer. Staying low reduces how much smoke you breathe in.

choices.text: Run through the corridor standing upright to save time
choices.feedback: Standing up puts your face directly in the thickest, most toxic smoke. Smoke is the leading cause of fire-related deaths, so staying low matters more than speed.

choices.text: Turn back and shelter in your office instead
choices.feedback: Sheltering in place is only advised when instructed by officials or when exits are fully blocked. Here, a viable escape route still exists, so retreating wastes it.
